articles.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.snippet: Megaspeed has been accused of funneling AI chips to China after a former executive's affair with Jensen Huang became public.
articles.full_text:
US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
- Published
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The US Department of Commerce announced on Monday that it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks, a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funneling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

articles.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drones in Libya, Zelensky says
articles.snippet: The Kremlin warns of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declines to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.
articles.full_text:
Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drones in Libya, Zelensky says
- Published
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
There was an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base in the early morning, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia, local authorities said.
Zelensky added that Ukraine's attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.
The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.
Libya's two governments - the UN-recognised government in the capital, Tripoli, and a rival administration in the east - have both condemned the attack.
The Tripoli foreign ministry said the country would not accept being drawn into the conflict.
It said foreign forces would not be allowed to use Libyan ports and civilian infrastructure for military purposes.
The eastern government, based in Benghazi, called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty.
Seven naval drones were deployed to target and sink the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, Zelensky said in a statement on Monday. He added that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed.
The Ukrainian president said the second ship was the MV ANGARA, a Russian container carrier.
The attack came the day after a Russian cargo vessel was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland. The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning.
Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely to be behind the attack. Kyiv has not commented.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that the "expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic" was a "dangerous trend" and has said "it is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region."
When questioned over the attacks in Libya, Peskov said information would be provided by the country's defence ministry and added: "We paid attention to Zelensky's statements about it".
Peskov declined to comment on the strikes on Russian ships in Libya and said that that information would be provided by Russia's Defence Ministry.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks on Sunday, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X., external
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.
US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.
Neither of Libya's rival administrations has formally declared support for either side in the Russia-Ukraine war, but they have contrasting ties with Moscow and Kyiv.
The head of the Libyan National Army, which controls much of the east of the country, has longstanding links with Russia.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
GNS has accused the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU) of hosting Ukrainian military personnel and allowing them to operate from Libyan territory against Russian targets.
Separately, the GNU warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
It said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.
As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Dr Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.
Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."

articles.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
articles.snippet: Ukraine's sinking of a Russian battleship at a port in Libya raises the stakes of the war a notch, writes Frank Gardner.
articles.full_text:
What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
- Published
Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.
The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.
Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks â what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" â have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.
The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.
And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".
Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.
Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
Impact elsewhere in Europe
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.
It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.
But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much â but not all â of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.
Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.
In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.
The three Baltic states â Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania â all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.
There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.
Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.
Hybrid attacks
Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.
It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.
This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.
There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

articles.title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
articles.snippet: Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were reportedly given 74 lashes in Qom.
articles.full_text:
Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
- Published
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.
There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.
"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).
Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.
In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".
Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.
Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.
In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.
According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

articles.title: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
articles.snippet: Interests of oil-producing countries, a US boycott and a dispute over finance may have torpedoed climate talks.
articles.full_text:
What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
- Published
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.
Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".
Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?
The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.
Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.
The wider political backdrop was still more revealing.
The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.
And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
A majority that may yet offer hope
Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.
Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action.
So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?
The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.
Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received.
"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.
Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."
Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.
The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.
So is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?
The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.
But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary.
Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.
Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels.
The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate.
Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed

Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31

A rare moment of agreement
Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.
The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5Â°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.
This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.
Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.
And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.
That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

articles.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.snippet: The report says there are signs of possible contamination across almost all of Gaza as a result of Israel's actions.
articles.full_text:
Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
- Published
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says, external.
Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".
In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards".
Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".
Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.
The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".
Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.
Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.
The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
The Israeli embassy sharply criticised the report, arguing that it relied on satellite imagery "and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny".
It said the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed.
Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.
A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.
"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."
At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.
Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

articles.title: India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
articles.snippet: As Nepal rebuilds after deadly floods, its prime minister sets contentious issues aside to secure Indian funding, port access and a new train service.
articles.full_text:
India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
- Published
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.
The contrast between the two leaders was striking.
Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (Â£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones.
The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan".
Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.
While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy.
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.
Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old.
His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.
According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs.
"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."
Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".
There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit.
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity.
The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita.
There was, however, disappointment on aviation.
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.
Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects.
"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat.
India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional.
"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough."
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

articles.title: Search and rescue teams race against time to find survivors after Nigeria boat tragedy
articles.snippet: The government blames overcrowding, poor maintenance, and missing life jackets for boat accidents.
articles.full_text:
Search and rescue teams race against time to find survivors after Nigeria boat tragedy
- Published
Nigerian search and rescue teams are racing against time to find survivors after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.
Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.
The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.
Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.
The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.
Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.
Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services.
"As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News.
"Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.
Why do Nigeria's boat disaster keep happening?
- Published20 July
Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets.
"Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.
There have been reports that the boat was carrying more than 300 people but the Nema spokesperson said this wasn't correct. He did not say how many people were on board but said it was overcrowded.
The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access.
"Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.
In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.
He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.
Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.
In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

US states sue SpaceX over Grok AI’s creation of child sexual abuse material
Virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday, accusing the company of promoting Grok’s ‘spicy mode’.
The US states of Virginia and Oregon have sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX, saying the business harmed consumers by avoiding safeguards when it designed and launched an artificial intelligence chatbot capable of creating sexualised images.
The attorneys general of both states filed complaints in separate lawsuits on Monday.
Recommended Stories

Several states had announced investigations into Grok over similar claims in recent months, but Virginia and Oregon are the first states to sue.
The lawsuits filed in state courts accuse SpaceX of misleading consumers about Grok’s safety and failing to put adequate safeguards in place while promoting its “spicy mode”. The feature allows users to take an existing photograph of a person and generate a sexual or nude image or video, according to the lawsuits.
The company prioritised its business model over the safety of millions of people, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in his state’s lawsuit.
“To push its lagging product, Grok, to tens of millions of new users, it stripped out industry-standard safeguards and marketed a ‘spicy mode’ built to produce nudity,” Jones said in the lawsuit. “For these Defendants, weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature.”
Virginia and Oregon accused SpaceX of violating their respective consumer protection laws. They are seeking damages, penalties and court orders forcing the company to stop violating state law.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Grok is available to users of X, the social media platform that is a subsidiary of SpaceX.

“The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards,” the company posted.

Investigators from the attorney general’s office in Virginia found that Grok’s image moderation was inconsistent, and that the bot would advise users on how to circumvent the moderation measures by avoiding words that triggered it, according to the lawsuit.
Beginning in January, Grok told users that its image generation features were only for paying subscribers, which did not stop the images’ creation but allowed the company to profit from them, the lawsuit said.
SpaceX is facing more than a dozen lawsuits brought by individuals who say nonconsensual sexual images of them as minors or adults were generated by Grok.

articles.title: US drug prices leave patients facing impossible choices
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Despite having jobs and health insurance, some of the US's sickest patients have trouble affording medicines they need.
articles.full_text:
US drug prices leave patients facing impossible choices
Despite working and having health insurance, some of the country’s sickest patients have trouble affording the medicines they need.
Sarah Wisniewski and her sister were once contemplating an extraordinary arrangement to manage their shared multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnoses: alternating months taking a life-changing medication.
The drug, which Wisniewski says costs thousands of dollars a month without insurance coverage, was so expensive that the sisters considered rationing their treatment rather than going without it entirely.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Trump proposes new rules to ban gender-affirming care for transgender youth
- list 2 of 3Failure of rival health bills underscores impasse in US politics
- list 3 of 3Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies amid historic US measles resurgence
“It’s a weird thing to have to think about,” the 45-year-old told Al Jazeera. “You go to college, you get insurance, you get a good job, you pay your bills, you do everything right and, still, you’re having to ration your medication.”
Wisniewski is one of more than four in 10 adults in the United States who did not take medication as prescribed last year because of the cost, estimates KFF, an independent health policy research organisation.
Her experience highlights the growing financial pressures facing some of the nation’s sickest patients, who have trouble affording costly prescription medications, despite having jobs and private health insurance.
‘Every spare dime’ needed for medications
Wisniewski was diagnosed with MS in 2017 after experiencing increasingly debilitating symptoms, including difficulties with her vision, mobility and breathing.
She became one of the nearly eight in 10 American adults who are living with at least one chronic condition, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
In the summer of 2024, her neurologist prescribed Kesimpta, a medication that, she says, dramatically improved her condition. But her insurance company, Blue Cross Blue Shield, notified her it would not cover the treatment.
Wisniewski appealed three times before requesting a hearing in her state of Maryland. Only weeks before that hearing was due to take place did her insurer agree to cover the medication.
Without that intervention, Wisniewski said, she would have faced a monthly bill of approximately $10,000.
The impact of obtaining treatment has been significant on her life.
“I went from barely being able to walk … Now, I walk my dog every morning, a mile-and-a-half to two miles,” she said.
Wisniewski has also been able to maintain her federal contracting job, which she described as highly technical and demanding.
But the financial burden remains substantial. Even with the help of insurance, Wisniewski estimates she spends between $800 and $900 each month on medication.
“Almost every spare dime I get is going to just keeping me healthy, so I can make it to work the next day,” she said.
‘A uniquely American problem’
Unlike many countries, particularly wealthier ones, the US allows pharmaceutical companies significantly more latitude to set their own prices.
According to the Patients For Affordable Drugs Now patient-advocacy organisation, current laws give manufacturers “unilateral power to set launch prices in the US and the ability to raise prices at will”.
“I believe this is a uniquely American problem, ”Wisniewski said. “Other countries are … able to provide for their citizens these drugs, if not for free, at an affordable level.”
The monthly cost of her medication in Canada is 2,333 Canadian dollars ($1,623). It’s even lower in Australia at 41 Australian dollars ($27) or 6.60 Australian dollars ($4.37) with a concession card, which allows eligible residents in the country to receive discounts on healthcare and prescription medicines.
The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA), a consortium that represents US drug companies, argues that a complicated network of third-party middlemen, known as pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), and insurance companies are to blame for the country’s high drug prices.
“PBMs and insurers control benefits through processes like prior authorisation, embedded step therapy, and formulary controls that may allow PBMs and insurers to deny coverage or push patients to alternative treatments from the initially prescribed medicine,” PhRMA’s website said. The organisation did not reply to a request for comment.
A study by the nonpartisan RAND organisation, released in 2024, found that US prescription drug prices were substantially higher than those in other wealthy countries, particularly for name-brand medications.
Using 2022 data, RAND’s researchers found that US manufacturers’ gross prices across all prescription drugs were 278 percent higher than the average prices in 33 other high-income countries. For brand-name drugs, US prices were more than four times the comparison-country average.
But the consequences of the current US system can extend far beyond the cost of individual prescriptions.
Wisniewski said the money she spends maintaining access to medication is money she cannot put toward local businesses, transportation or investments in her community.
“I really think that a lot of people, at an abstract level, understand that this could happen to anybody at any point in time,” she said. “But I don’t think that it really hits home to folks that you are legitimately one bad phone call away from losing everything.”
What can be done?
After this month’s historic midterm elections in the US, where Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress by wide margins, there will be few areas of agreement with Democrats’ Republican counterparts – and President Donald Trump.
But targeted reforms that address the high cost of prescriptions could be an area where both parties find common ground.
A survey conducted by Fabrizio Ward in March 2025 found more than three in four voters – including 70 percent of Trump supporters – wanted Congress to take action on reducing drug prices.
The issue was the focus of a US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday of last week, when lawmakers and healthcare experts examined how pharmaceutical companies and insurers influence pricing and access to medication.
At that November 17 hearing, witnesses highlighted several factors contributing to high prescription drug costs, including pharmaceutical patent protections and the role of PBMs.
Merith Basey, chief executive officer of Patients For Affordable Drugs Now, argued that pharmaceutical companies exploit the patent system to delay competition from cheaper alternatives.
One of those practices, known as patent thicketing, involves companies securing multiple patents covering different aspects of a medication or its delivery device, potentially making it more difficult for competitors to introduce generic alternatives.
Basey told lawmakers the introduction of generic competition could substantially reduce prices, arguing a single generic competitor can lower a drug’s price by 39 percent, while six or more competitors can reduce prices by as much as 95 percent.
But other witnesses pointed to PBMs, claiming their involvement in distributing drugs can influence pricing.
The Senate panel has advanced a number of proposals to tackle the high cost of prescription drugs in the US. One of those is the bipartisan Eliminating Thickets to Improve Competition (ETHIC) Act, which would limit the practice of patent thickening, making it easier for generic drugs to enter the US market and lower costs.
“Big Pharma knows exactly what it’s doing in monopolising the US patent system: driving up drug costs for Americans while preventing generic-drug manufacturers from getting their foot in the market,” Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, one of the bill’s sponsors, said in a statement.
Wisniewski noted that while the ETHIC Act wouldn’t make her prescription “cheap”, it would be “astronomically better than what we have now”.

Questions are being asked about how the big cat arrived, with suspicion falling on the country’s growing role as a hub for wild-animal smuggling.
Police and animal welfare teams have launched a hunt for a lioness reported to be prowling the outskirts of Istanbul.
City authorities closed a woodland area in the northern Sariyer district on Monday as the teams expanded a search for the big cat, which was spotted in the area the previous evening.

Turkiye’s National Parks Directorate said on Sunday that police officers in Zekeriyakoy, north of Istanbul’s European side, had reported spotting “an animal resembling a lion” on surveillance cameras.
Grainy security camera footage republished by Turkish media appeared to show what looked like a big cat prowling across a patch of open countryside.

articles.title: China’s fourth aircraft carrier, bigger than others and nuclear-powered, nears completion
articles.snippet: China’s fourth aircraft carrier, a gigantic vessel known so far as just Type 004, will come out as early as next year bigger than its predecessors and with nuclear power that can launch planes faster than usual in case of any conflict, analysts say.
articles.full_text:
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — China’s fourth aircraft carrier, a gigantic vessel known so far as just Type 004, will come out as early as next year bigger than its predecessors and with nuclear power that can launch planes faster than usual in case of any conflict, analysts say.
And it’s tipped to add pressure on countries, such as Japan and the United States, that already keep a high alert for the Chinese military.
The carrier being built now in the northern port city Dalian could accommodate 75 to 90 planes once deployed, the Asia program director at the think tank Defence Priorities has said.
As of October, the vessel’s hull measured about 322 meters in length from the unfinished bow to stern with a width of approximately 46 meters, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), also a think tank.
CSIS called Type 004 “far larger than any other class of surface combatant” in China’s navy.
Aerial photos of the carrier show the “basic hull form” already built, auguring well for a 2027 launch, said Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Deployment would take five to 10 years, he said.
The specs would make Type 004 “slightly larger” than China’s Fujian aircraft carrier, currently the biggest one in its fleet, Koh said.
Information available today about the Type 004 – likely to be renamed after a Chinese province like the existing three – classify the vessel as a “supercarrier” in terms of electronics, tonnage and aircraft carrying capacity, said Alexander Huang, chairman of the Council of Strategic and Wargaming Studies in Taipei.
Nuclear power on board would offer the aircraft more propulsion than China’s existing electromagnetic aircraft launch system, Koh said. He said that would eliminate the need for power generators on board the carrier while allowing faster takeoffs – without payload compromises – and quick combat turnarounds for refueling.
“It seems to signal a certain strategic objective,” Koh said of the nuclear capability. “It’s not just going to move along your coast. It seems to signal a certain global ambition.”
Nuclear power will give the carrier “essentially unlimited endurance” and allow for global deployment without the kind of tanker support a conventionally powered carrier needs, said David Silbey, a Cornell University professor specializing in military history and defense policy.
The fourth carrier may get posted to northern China because the other three are in the south, Huang said. In that scenario, he said, China could “use one of the four to always operate somewhere.”
Type 004 may be used for training and maintenance as well as operations, Huang added.
China’s fourth carrier gets it closer to rivaling the U.S. navy, analysts said.
It will compare in size to the Nimitz and Ford class U.S. carriers, which means it can carry as many as 100 aircraft, Silbey said. “That gives it much more striking power than previous carriers, which could only carry around 50,” he said.
The U.S. navy has 11 carriers, all nuclear powered.
Even if smaller than the U.S. fleet, a Chinese navy with nuclear-powered carriers can mount a challenge to the United States, Koh said.
The U.S. navy maintains bases in Guam, Hawaii and Japan plus treaty alliances with Japan and the Philippines. The U.S. and China have long seen each other as rival superpowers.
Experts have said China sent an especially large number of its naval deployments near Japan’s southernmost islands and nearby waters since a political rift that erupted in November 2025 over a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
The Philippines is embroiled in a maritime sovereignty dispute with China.
China plans to build more carriers over the next decade for a “blue water capability that they’ve never really had before,” Silbey said. “In the Pacific, it means that they can go after American assets that are out of range of their other assets.”

articles.title: Ukraine confirms it sank Russian corvette in Libyan port
articles.snippet: Ukraine was behind the explosive sinking of the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi over the weekend, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, and the country’s military released accompanying videos.
articles.full_text:
GLASGOW, Scotland — Ukraine was behind the explosive sinking of the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi over the weekend, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, and the country’s military released accompanying videos.
The Merkury, a warship that had been acquired by the Russian navy in 2023, was left mostly submerged after sea drones struck it on Nov. 22. The video released by Ukrainian authorities shows several of the uncrewed, explosive-laden boats slamming into the side of the moored ship.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) says it carried out the operation jointly with Ukraine’s Defense Forces. Zelenskyy said seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were used in the operation and that a Ka-27 helicopter aboard the corvette was also destroyed.
During the same operation, the Russian dry-cargo ship MV Angara was also targeted. The SBU describes Angara as a sanctioned vessel used to move weapons and military equipment on Russian routes to Syria and Libya, and says Merkury had escorted it.
Reuters, citing local medical sources, reported ten injuries in the attack, including Russians and Libyans. Al Jazeera reported one person had been killed.
Satellite imagery taken by U.S. commercial imagery provider Planet and reviewed by Defense News showed a ship ablaze in the port of Benghazi, with a long smoke trail. Additional satellite imagery shared online by open-source investigators appeared to confirm that the ship had been sunk.
The attack is one of the most stark examples of geographic spillover of the war in Ukraine. Libya is particularly fertile ground for a confrontation between Ukraine and Russia, given the country’s unresolved political division: The east, centered on Benghazi, is controlled by the Government of National Stability, backed by Russia, while the western half of the country, centered on Tripoli, is under the control of the internationally recognized Government of National Unity.
The United Nations, which maintains an “advanced mission” for the post-conflict settlement in Libya, put out a statement saying that “Libya can not afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”
Reporting has suggested that in addition to spillover of direct confrontation between Russia and Ukraine, the two countries may increasingly be engaged in proxy conflicts across Africa. In Mali, where the Russian Africa Corps – the successor to the paramilitary Wagner Group, now incorporated into the military – backs the government, Ukraine appears to be sharing intelligence and even sending operatives in support of the opposing side.
And in the weeks before Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad fell in December 2024, Ukrainian military intelligence reportedly sent about 20 drone operators and 150 drones to assist Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), the group that led the offensive against Assad’s Russian-backed government.

articles.title: $16 billion propulsion mega-contract posted in error, Air Force says

articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Air Force is walking back an award announcement it made in error for a massive contract vehicle worth up to $16.1 billion for propulsion work, a service spokesperson told Breaking Defense.
On Nov. 20, the Air Force announced it had picked 58 companies for the service’s Advanced Propulsion Acquisition Contract (APAC), set to run through 2041. The program is structured as an indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract, meaning the Air Force is not necessarily obligated to spend its full amount.
That award, published on the Pentagon’s daily contract roundup, was posted erroneously, an Air Force spokesperson confirmed today, though the service is planning to eventually award the contract.
“Once awarded, APAC will serve as an agile, enterprise-level contracting vehicle for propulsion requirements across all lifecycle phases, including science and technology, research and development, test and evaluation, production, sustainment, and modernization,” the Air Force said in a statement to Breaking Defense.
The Air Force additionally confirmed that a total of 58 vendors so far are planned for selection, and that an initial $1,000 disbursement to each will “support participation” in a post-award orientation conference for the winners.
“Future orders will be competed among the qualified vendor pool as requirements are validated and funded. Specific platforms, scope, funding, contract type, period of performance, and pricing will be established at the individual Delivery Order or Task Order level,” the statement reads.
The vendor pool from the Nov. 20 contract notice features a range of firms, from startups to established engine primes with different areas of propulsion expertise. And the award comes as the Air Force seeks new and more effective ways to power its existing and future platforms, from drone wingmen to large mobility aircraft.
The Air Force has recently tapped several vendors to open up options for different sizes of drones and missiles, and is also developing an advanced engine that could power future platforms like the F-47 stealth fighter.

articles.title: Colombia races for counter-drone tech as militant groups embrace drones as frontline weapons
articles.snippet: “As knowledge of drone tactics proliferates faster than governments can deploy countermeasures, it seems likely we will begin to see them crop up in more countries in the region,” one analyst told Breaking Defense.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Earlier this month, drones flew over a military base in Santa Rosa del Sur, in Colombia’s Bolívar department, dropping explosives that killed three soldiers when detonated.
Just days before that in October, the Colombian military said a vessel assigned to Riverine Marine Battalion No. 42 was attacked in the Guapi River in a similar fashion, killing one Marine and injuring four others.
In September, a civilian radar in the Valle del Cauca region was damaged after what appeared to be an explosive-laden drone reportedly collided with it.
And a new attack occurred just this Saturday evening: the headquarters of a battalion in La Jagua de Ibirico, César department, were attacked with drones and explosives. One soldier died and at least 12 were wounded.
The incidents, analysts say, are the latest examples of militant groups operating drones in ways that mirror battlefield uses — leaving local governments to race to catch up with the technology needed to defend against them. And Colombia appears to be ground zero for what could emerged as a new wave of conflict against rebels and narco groups in South and Central America.
The explosive-carrying drones are “inexpensive, easy to acquire and useful for monitoring security forces and protecting illicit operations,” Rebecca Bill Chavez, former US deputy assistant secretary for defense for Western Hemisphere Affairs, told Breaking Defense.
Use of small drones by militant and drug-trafficking groups isn’t new, but Chavez, the president of the Inter American Dialogue, said a growing problem is that the groups “have gone from using drones to monitor troop movements to launching coordinated attacks with multiple drones,” including unmanned systems using fiber-optic guidance systems.
Colombia has emerged as the flash point since August, when a new government led by President Abelardo de la Espriella promised a “mano dura” — or strong hand — approach to countering cartel and other armed groups. The Colombian armed forces have carried out several major operations, including air strikes, against historic rebel groups like the ELN and FARC, as well as drug cartels like the Clan del Golfo, and other non-state criminal networks. (Each of the named groups have been declared a terrorist organization by the US State Department.)
In response, during just the first 100 days of de la Espriella’s term, Colombia has suffered at least 93 attacks that involved drones, according to country’s news agency Caracol Radio. Of the 26 Army personnel killed during these 100 days, “at least 11” were killed due to drone-dropped explosives. (Colombian insurgents generally do not take responsibility for drone attacks, with the government usually assigning blame.)
On Nov. 8, the Ministry of Defense announced the seizure of a weapons cache, property of the Clan del Golfo, which included one drone and 35 grenades “conditioned to be dropped by this [uncrewed] aircraft,” suggesting that local insurgent groups are still investing in these weapons.
“There is no conventional drone warfare in Colombia,” a Colombian former army colonel told Breaking Defense on the condition of anonymity. “Rather, there are sporadic attacks against units in frontline areas which have no c-UAS [counter-unmanned aerial systems] protection.”
Counter Options
The surge in drone threats is likely to lead to greater investment in counter-drone systems.
The previous president, Gustavo Petro, announced Bogotá would create an “anti-drone shield” that would include fixed, mobile and man-portable counter-drone systems. But Colombia’s new defense minister, Jorge Eduardo Mora, said the effort hadn’t amounted to much by the time the new administration came in.
The Colombian armed forces do operate some counter-UAS systems. The Defense Ministry released photos of soldiers with jamming rifles on Nov. 8, stating that troops in the Chocó department had neutralized a drone to prevent “grenades from being dropped on soldiers.”
However, more systems are needed. The retired colonel explained to Breaking Defense that the armed forces require “air defense systems specifically for drone threats, both mobile and fixed.” Chavez agreed, saying “investing in counter-drone defenses is essential to protect soldiers, police, and civilians.”
One potential remedy, according to Henry Ziemer of the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, would be for Colombia to join the US-run drone and counter-drone marketplace, as Argentina, Mexico and Panama have reportedly done. In August, the US military sent out the first “tranche” of invitations to “selected international partners” with a second tranche to follow.
But relations between Washington and Bogotá may have become more complicated this month after The New York Times reported that de la Espriella had rebuffed an American offer of joint counter-drug operations — though de la Espriella denied the report. On Friday, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrapped up a Central and South American tour, praising the closeness of US and Colombian militaries.
Still, getting help with counter-drone capabilities from the US or elsewhere and training up Colombian soldiers is only “part of the answer,” Chavez said.
“Without stronger intelligence and investigative capabilities, governments will keep responding to attacks without stopping the criminal organizations behind them,” she said.
“Who is supplying and modifying these drones? Who is training the operators?” she asked. “The goal should be to dismantle those networks, not just shoot down drones once they’re airborne.”
The retired Colombian colonel, a Lancero, said he agreed. The Ministry of Defense and other agencies “need to strengthen intelligence operations to locate where the narco-insurgents’ drone bases are,” he said.
And it’s not just Colombia. So far, drones carrying lethal explosives have also been used in attacks in Brazil and Mexico. Ziemer is pessimistic about the future.
“As knowledge of drone tactics proliferates faster than governments deploy countermeasures, it seems likely we will begin to see them crop up in more countries in the region.”

articles.title: Congress is ‘out of time’ to decide on reconciliation, needs to settle topline spending: Sen. Coons
articles.snippet: “If we could get to a bipartisan topline, we could spend the time from Thanksgiving to the end of the year getting a lot of this finished,” said Sen. Chris Coons, the top democrat on the Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee.
articles.full_text:
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia — The clock has run out on getting lawmakers to back a $350 billion reconciliation bill for the Pentagon, a democratic senator said, likely leaving it to Democrats to sort through the funding mess next year.
“We’re out of time for reconciliation,” Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, the top democrat on the Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee, told reporters here Saturday. “The final bill will be closer to a trillion than $1.5 [trillion]. And at this point, it’ll almost certainly get done next year in a new Congress.”
His comments capped off a week of speculation on Capitol Hill over the state of the administration’s $1.5 trillion fiscal 2027 ask for the Pentagon. That request revolves around $1.15 trillion in the base budget and $350 billion in a separate reconciliation bill that includes big-ticket items like Golden Dome, drones and multi-year munition buys.
Right now, the clock is ticking on a path ahead. The department is being funded with a continuing resolution that runs out Dec. 11, meaning lawmakers now need to pass another CR or defense spending bill to avoid facing a department shutdown. Democrats are also poised to take the gavels in both chambers on Jan. 3, giving them more power to use the spending bills to cut off funds for the Iran war and reshuffle spending priorities.
But from his perch, Coons urged lawmakers not to wait. Right now, he said, the top priority should be agreeing on topline spending numbers and acknowledging that reconciliation is “dead.”
“If we could get to a bipartisan topline, we could spend the time from Thanksgiving to the end of the year getting a lot of this finished,” he added. “But we still don’t have a topline agreement between the defense and non-defense portions, and that’s the most critical thing now.”
Once that figure is in place, both chambers can continue to refine their respective plans for FY27. In the Senate last week, appropriators released a defense spending bill that centered on a topline of $1.1 trillion. This summer, the House Appropriations Committee released its $1 trillion defense spending bill for FY27. Neither have been approved by the full chamber and could significantly change depending on when the bill is passed and the ultimate topline.
From his vantage point, Coons called the Pentagon’s FY27 strategy “sloppy, unprofessional, [and] at times incoherent” since an “enormous” amount of the reconciliation ask should have been requested in the base bill, a move lawmakers are now trying to rectify.
“We have had a good and collaborative bipartisan process between the House and the Senate, the majority and the minority, on moving lots of programs and money [into the base bill],” Coons told reporters. “There is still a fair amount of work to be done.”
When asked about the prospect of forgoing a FY27 defense spending bill and keeping the department at FY26 funding levels via a full-year CR, Coons told reporters that “should not” be the plan.
As lawmakers work through FY27 spending plans, a separate $87.6 billion supplemental request that includes $67.1 billion in defense funds to cover expenses associated with the war in Iran is also withering on Capitol Hill.
Coons said democrats could be on board with passing a version of the request to replenish weapons stockpiles and boost counter-drone defenses if they could ensure the dollars would not be spent to keep the war going.
“My caucus has had the consistent position: Unless there’s an end to this war with Iran, we’re not providing supplemental funding,” Coons added. “There are demonstrable needs … some of us would be willing to fund.”

articles.title: Umbra, ICEYE tout higher-resolution radar imaging with new satellites
articles.snippet: Both companies are now offering resolutions significantly lower than the previous industry standard of around 25 centimeters, allowing customers to see smaller ground targets with higher fidelity.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Two of the world’s most prominent synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging firms, Umbra and ICEYE, are now offering government and commercial customers higher-resolution imagery as the international market for remote sensing satellite services expands.
California-based Umbra debuted its new Freetail satellite model today, promising performance levels commensurate with much larger satellites in a spacecraft weighing 200 kilogram (about 441 pounds). The satellites will be able to produce images with resolutions down to five centimeters. The first of these new satellites, called Freetail 5, is slated to fly in 2028, according to the company’s announcement.
On Nov. 16, Finnish SAR-sat maker ICEYE separately announced its Gen5 satellites, which the company says can provide government customers with imagery at resolutions as fine as 11 centimeters, subject to regional spectrum management rules set by the International Telecommunication Union. Commercial customers are being offered SAR images with 16 centimeter resolution, with services expected to begin next year, the company said.
Both companies also are touting their satellites’ reprogrammable software and onboard processing chops, as well as increases in the number of times an image can be processed during each satellite’s orbit.
The announcements come as the market for Earth imaging is booming, with governments — particularly in Europe — rushing to acquire sovereign capabilities. SAR imaging is particularly useful for European customers given the region’s frequent cloud cover, which can limit the effectiveness of traditional optical imaging satellites.
For its part, Umbra is targeting its pitch toward the United States and its allies, especially military and intelligence services.
“With four times the radar power, twice the antenna area and hourly global revisit, Freetail 5 is designed to collect more across greater areas to deliver unprecedented operational value,” Umbra CEO David Langan said in a statement. “Freetail 5 represents a new standard for space-based intelligence that will create significant advantage for the United States and its allies.”
ICEYE is pitching Gen5 to a broader customer base, including civil, commercial and military markets. The company is also highlighting its plans to incorporate an onboard artificial intelligence processor “that will, over time, unlock screening, pre-processing and tip-and-cue directly on the satellite, rather than waiting for data to reach the ground,” according to the company announcement.
Rafal Modrzewski, ICEYE’s CEO and co-founder, said: “Time to decision is everything in space-based intelligence, whether you’re tracking a vessel or responding to a flood. Gen5 shortens it at every step: sharper and more images per pass, and AI analysis that starts in orbit.”
