articles.title: Yes, no, maybe? The countries that can (or can’t) deliver Ukraine’s 40 requested F-16s
articles.snippet: “Forty F-16s is a legitimate request, and there is an urgency, but it is an ambitious, big number and definitely not easy to get them in Ukraine, especially in a short period of time,” analyst Federico Borsari told Breaking Defense.
articles.full_text:
MILAN and BELFAST — Last week, as Russian drones and missiles rained down on Ukrainian territory, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pleaded with European heads of state for more F-16s to defend the country — with a very specific number.
“The F-16s we have now… spend a lot of time being repaired instead of flying. So we need more fighter jets. More F-16s… I’m grateful to every country in our Air Force Coalition. A lot has already been done, but we need to do more. Specifically, we need 40 more F-16s,” Zelenskyy said at the 37th Ukraine Defense Contact Group (UDCG) meeting on Tuesday in the Ramstein format.
That raises two questions: First, why 40? Second, which countries could realistically deliver this many aircraft?
While the Ukrainian government does not publish an official inventory of its aerial arsenal, the aviation publication AeroCorner, citing open-source databases, estimated that as of Sept. 2026, Ukraine possesses 39 F-16AM Fighting Falcons. It reported that by the end of 2025, these aircraft were flying around 80 percent of all the country’s Air Force sorties, including all mission types. (FlightGlobal’s World Air Force 2026 directory says Ukraine has 35 of the older F-16A models; a small discrepancy between the two datasets makes sense given the opaque nature of information out of Ukraine).
To Zelenskyy’s point, a recent report published by the London-based Royal United Services Institute emphasized the role of Western fighter jets, including the F-16s, to shoot down Russian drones. If the jets are forced into service for that mission, it means heavy wear and tear on expensive and rare assets that Ukraine could be using elsewhere. Hence, Kyiv seeking to roughly double its fleet makes sense — though likely won’t be easy.
The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense did not respond to a request for comment on why 40 jets is the target. Federico Borsari, a defense analyst with the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Breaking Defense that while 40 planes were a “legitimate request,” it was also “an ambitious, big number and definitely not easy to get them in Ukraine, especially in a short period of time.”
So, where could they come from? The obvious answer would be to look first to the United States, the largest operator (and sole producer) of the F-16. However, aside from some non-operational airframes, Washington has been unwilling to provide Ukraine with fighter aircraft from its own fleet. So Kyiv will instead look once more to its European supporters.
According to the ubiquitous tracker F-16.net, at the time of writing, eight European countries (outside Ukraine) operate or are introducing the fighter jets into active military service, and three others — Norway, the Netherlands, and Denmark — have retired them.
After Tuesday’s meeting, only Belgium was officially listed as willing to provide F-16s—10 by the end of the year. Brussels announced back in 2024 that it would eventually give Ukraine 30 F-16s as the military transitions its fighter fleet to the F-35, also made by Lockheed Martin. According to FlightGlobal’s directory, Belgium has 52 F-16s (44 F-16AMs and 8 F-16BMs) and is expected to reach full operational readiness of its F-35 fleet in 2030 (ordered 34 F-35As and plans to acquire 11 more).
As for any additional F-16s, Bosari said that even if European countries agree to send planes to Ukraine, several factors would make such deliveries complex in the short term, from the need to modernize some jets to reactivate retired ones, secure third-party transfer authorization (as with Belgian F-16s), and complete lengthy maintenance work.
There may also be a time crunch for Zelenskyy, Borsari said, thanks to upcoming elections in some European nations are another factor likely to affect or complicate potential fighter deliveries.
“In some countries, such as France, [which pledged at the UDCG meeting to send two Mirage 2000-5F to Ukraine by the end of 2026], where elections are coming up, it might be more complex to justify these transfers in the eyes of the population. I’m not saying it won’t happen, but there is a political dimension to these agreements that are also politically sensitive in some nations,” the expert said.
Three European countries operating F-16 fighter jets — Greece, Slovakia, and Poland — have scheduled national parliamentary elections in 2027.
Here is what to know about the state of the rest of Europe’s F-16 fleets.
A Couple Hard Nos
Nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, several European nations appear to be at a crossroads, asking themselves whether they can release any operational fighter jets without weakening or altogether putting at risk their own air forces.
While most countries didn’t immediately respond to Zelenskyy’s 40-plane request, Portugal went ahead and ruled out sending F-16 jets to Ukraine, with Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Ranger calling such a transfer “essentially impossible” during a press conference in Kyiv last week because the country needs its existing aircraft to protect its own territory.
Greece, one of Europe’s largest F-16 operators, received about 170 fighter jets in different configurations between the 1990s and 2010 and has since undergone a major modernization program. But it has maintained its decision not to transfer any aircraft to Kyiv, opting instead to focus on helping to train Ukrainian pilots and technicians.
Norway retired its F-16 fleet in 2022 after more than 40 years of service, sold 32 to Romania and has already donated six to Ukraine. But the Norwegian Ministry of Defense told Breaking Defense no other F-16s will be forthcoming.
“The remaining [F-16] airframes are not assessed as viable to return to operational service and will be used for purposes such as maintenance training and museum display,” the ministry said.
The Undeclared, And The Unlikely
At this week’s Ramstein meeting, Denmark committed €200 million ($218 million) for air defense and a €645 million package of drones and F-16 ammunition, but did not say whether it would send more F-16s to Kyiv than it already promised. The Scandinavian country has previously said it would transfer up to 19, with the first deliveries made in 2024.
Romania has spent significant effort building its F-16 fleet, which represents the only combat-ready jets the country has, relied on for air policing across the Black Sea. At the same time, it waits for its own F-35 deliveries, expected to start in the early 2030s. As such, it is not likely to be in a position to transfer a significant number of fighters. Romania’s defense ministry did not respond to a request for comment at press time.
Since the onset of the war, Turkey, which possesses the second-largest F-16 fleet in all of NATO, has not publicly committed to send any of its aircraft to Ukraine, focusing rather on drone and armored vehicle donations. The Turkish MoD did not provide comments on the matter at the time of writing.
Slovakia received its full fleet of new F-16 Block 70 fighters this year and ordered four additional ones in September to replace the aging MiG-29s it sent to Ukraine in 2023. But since then, Slovakia’s stance has hardened as the current government has halted most military assistance to Kyiv. The Slovak Ministry of Defense did not respond to a request for comment at press time on whether this remains its position.
Similarly, Poland has previously opted to transfer MiG-29s rather than its F-16s to Ukraine. In 2023, Wojciech Skurkiewicz, Secretary of State at the Ministry of National Defense, told the Polish Parliament that “there was no discussion about handing over F-16 aircraft to the Ukrainian side.” It remains unclear whether this decision has changed. The Polish MoD did not respond to a request for comment at press time.
The Netherlands retired its F-16 in 2024 and completed deliveries of its 24 pledged jets to Ukraine a year later. The country has also supported Kyiv by providing retired aircraft for training and, in February, announced plans to supply F-16 simulators. However, it appears the Dutch have no F-16s left to send to Kyiv, having handed 18 to a training center in Romania for a symbolic one-euro sum in November 2025. The Dutch defense ministry did not respond to a request for comment at press time.
Bulgaria has ordered F-16 Block 70 jets, but local reports note that a delay to a second batch of eight aircraft has led Sofia to explore options for a second-hand fighter jet. The Eastern European country’s political support for military aid supplies to Ukraine is waning, with Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev reportedly stopping weapons and ammunition transfers because of budgetary issues. The country’s MoD did not respond to a request for comment at press time.

articles.title: Despite Hegseth memo, Canada hasn’t seen changes to defense relationship with US, says DefMin
articles.snippet: Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell told Breaking Defense the department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible US defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”
articles.full_text:
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia — Canada was caught off guard with news that the US was changing its defense relationship with its neighbor to the north, but its minister of National Defense said that so far, he has not seen a change in the military-to-military relationship.
“It’s clear that there’s some sort of document we haven’t seen, not aware of the contents of it,” David McGuinty said during a press conference on the sidelines of the Halifax International Security Forum. “But I can assure Canadians, and I can assure anybody who’s interested, that Canadian-American cooperation on defense, security, and intelligence continues.”
The Washington Post first reported on Friday evening that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had imposed new restrictions on the US-Canada defense relationship in a classified memo.
When asked about the memo, Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell told Breaking Defense the department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible US defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.
“DoW [Department of War] is prioritizing opportunities for bilateral cooperation that strengthens the defense of our Homelands and shared hemisphere, while supporting Canada’s ability to meet NATO obligations,” he said.
While Parnell did not disclose what changes may be coming to US-Canadian defense relations he said Hegseth’s “guidance” does not impact defense intelligence cooperation, binational North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) command, or cooperation through NATO.
At a separate press conference today, Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., said he reached out to administration officials and has been told the memo does not have any operational impact on DoD personnel that are in Canada today nor does it impact NORAD, NATO operations or Five Eyes.
“It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance DoD objectives,” Rounds told reporters. “They must request permission for Canadian think tank events or social engagements.”
News of the possible relationship shift comes as the neighbors remain locked in a trade war, and as Ottawa is moving out with a new Canadian Defence Industrial Strategy designed, in part, to depend less on US defense contractors by growing production capability at home.
While McGuinty said the defense relationship with the United States “remains strong” he also reasserted ambitions to buy fewer weapons from Washington.
“We’d like to procure less from the United States when it comes to military hardware and produce more of our own here in 10 core areas,” he told reporters. “And, if we can’t produce it here, we will partner with like-minded partners. And if we can’t partner, we will then buy as a third option.”
As part of the investment plan, McGuinty used this year’s annual event in Halifax to announce plans to join the NATO innovation fund — a multi-sovereign venture capital fund backed by a couple dozen NATO Allies. The initial plan, he said, is to contribute $100 million CAD ($69.72 million USD), to open up new opportunities for investment in Canadian startups and innovation funds.
“For Canadian innovators, that means new investment, new partnerships, and access to international markets,” McGuinty said. “For Canadian workers, it means good jobs in a growing industry, and for our armed forces, it means access to cutting-edge technologies and capabilities faster.”

articles.title: Hackers breach Austrian Foreign Ministry website, access diplomats' contact details
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Austria's Foreign Ministry said late last week that hackers breached one of its websites and accessed the names and official contact information of employees at its Vienna headquarters and at Austria’s diplomatic missions abroad.
articles.full_text:
Hackers breach Austrian Foreign Ministry website, access diplomats' contact details
Austria's Foreign Ministry said late last week that hackers breached one of its websites and accessed the names and official contact information of employees at its Vienna headquarters and at Austria’s diplomatic missions abroad.
The breach occurred between November 12 and 13 and affected a website operated by an external service provider, according to a ministry statement reported by public broadcaster ORF on Friday.
The ministry said the breach had been contained and that no personal information belonging to members of the public was compromised. The hackers have not been identified, and it remains unclear how they gained access to the website or whether they stole any information.
The ministry said it was taking the incident "very seriously" and had notified Austria's cybersecurity and data protection authorities.
A spokesperson told Recorded Future News: “For security reasons, we do not disclose details of specific technical vulnerabilities or security measures. The incident has not been attributed to any particular actor.”
The attack coincided with a global Microsoft service outage that disrupted several of the company's services for approximately 24 hours. Microsoft attributed the disruption to a software bug and infrastructure failures. Austrian authorities have not established whether the two incidents were connected.
Austria's Foreign Ministry has previously been targeted by suspected state-sponsored hackers linked to Moscow.
In late 2019 and early 2020, the ministry suffered a cyberattack that lasted several weeks and was described by Austria's National Security Council as a targeted intelligence-gathering operation. In July 2026, Vienna publicly attributed the attack to Russia.
The latest breach comes amid worsening diplomatic relations between Austria and Russia.
In October, Vienna expelled four Russian diplomats, bringing the number of Russian diplomatic personnel declared persona non grata by Austria since 2020 to 18.
Tensions escalated further last week after a Russian drone strike damaged the Austrian Embassy in Kyiv. Austria condemned the strike as "unacceptable" and "a violation of international law," and Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger summoned Russia's ambassador in Vienna.
There is no public evidence linking Russia to the latest cyberattack. Moscow has repeatedly denied allegations of involvement in cyberattacks against European countries.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Signal blocks screenshots by Apple, Google operating systems to protect data from AI agents
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Google’s Gemini Intelligence and Apple's Siri AI "are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy," Signal said.
articles.full_text:
Signal blocks screenshots by Apple, Google operating systems to protect data from AI agents
The encrypted messaging platform Signal has announced it will by default stop users from taking screenshots of messages if they are using Google or Apple operating systems, a move fueled by concerns about how the tech giants deploy artificial intelligence agents.
Last year, the widely used messaging app restricted Microsoft 11 users from screenshotting and keeping messages. Similar restrictions will now apply to Google’s Gemini Intelligence and Apple's Siri AI, Signal Foundation president Meredith Whittaker said in a Friday blog post.
“These agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy,” the blog post said. “This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.”
Whittaker said Signal plans to specifically restrict the agentic systems integrated into iOS 27 and versions of Android where Signal detects AI assistants trying to read text.
The operating systems’ AI agents attempt to glean information from users by scanning what’s on their screens, Whittaker said, and in doing so hoover up the data in order to “answer your questions and do your bidding,” the blog post said.
Whittaker warned the agents are making the captured data accessible to random local databases and remote servers at random.
“All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation,” the blog post said.
While screenshots won’t be permitted by default, the blog post said users who choose to can disable the block in settings.
The “remedy is incomplete,” Whittaker warned, because blocking screenshots does not address “other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.”
The dearth of effective tools available to Signal and other app developers to use to stop AI agents from weakening privacy is a significant concern, the blog post said.
Whittaker condemned Microsoft, Apple and Google for failing to provide app developers with a mechanism to block agents’ access to data without significantly compromising the “core user experience.”
The same lack of cooperation from tech giants is also to blame for Signal’s inability to place the restrictions on macOS, the blog post said. Additionally, Signal has struggled with a profound lack of documentation about how the agents function.
“Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us,” Whittaker said.
“These three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem,” the blog post said of Apple, Google and Microsoft. “These agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy.”
Whittaker called on the companies to provide an easy way for users to opt-out of data access permissions tools, stop third-party agents from accessing data without users’ consent and bolster documentation lending transparency to how agents work.
Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Microsoft and Google declined to comment.
Meta also has been under fire, following recent reports that its AI agent Muse broke into Signal conversations and digest them
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: FBI reportedly facing second data breach involving National Crime Information Center
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The FBI is reportedly investigating a data breach involving the National Crime Information Center, a database used by U.S. law enforcement agencies that contains information on criminals, fugitives and missing people.
articles.full_text:
FBI reportedly facing second data breach involving National Crime Information Center
The FBI is reportedly investigating a data breach involving the National Crime Information Center, a database used by U.S. law enforcement agencies that contains information on criminals, fugitives and missing people.
The FBI did not respond to requests for comment but sources told CNN and later the Associated Press that the cyberattack took place on Thursday.
The database, known as the NCIC, is used among local, state and federal agencies to share information on criminals and investigations. It offers law enforcement agencies data on outstanding warrants and contains sensitive information of value to criminals and others.
President Donald Trump told Fox News this weekend that he had been briefed on the incident, adding: “I will say that it’s not good — I don’t like that.” He went on to say the breach may allow the public to have access to investigative files related to him.
If confirmed, this would be the second cybersecurity incident affecting the FBI this year. In September, the ShinyHunters hacking group breached the FBI’s job site and allegedly stole troves of information on every FBI employee.
Multiple people were arrested as part of the investigation into the ShinyHunters breach, including a cybersecurity expert from Canada.
The U.S. government has suffered from several cybersecurity incidents this year in addition to the attacks on the FBI.
Last month, hackers took down a platform used by all federal bankruptcy courts across the country and a ransomware attack in August targeted the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF). The ATF called the breach a “major incident” and said it involved a computer system containing information about targets of investigations.
The departments of Defense and Transportation also experienced cybersecurity incidents this year, and the Department of Agriculture was forced to take offline multiple systems used to facilitate payments between the agency and farmers after a cyberattack last week.

articles.snippet: “We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen,” CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said.
articles.full_text:
CrowdStrike to purchase Zscaler for $43.9 billion
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike will acquire cloud security company Zscaler for $43.9 billion in an all-stock deal announced on Monday morning.
The deal will see two of the largest cybersecurity companies consolidate, merging Zscaler’s tools with CrowdStrike’s suite of cyberattack response services, endpoint security platforms, and threat intelligence offerings. Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry will continue to run Zscaler and will join CrowdStrike’s board of directors.
CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said the acquisition of Zscaler will allow them to build “cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely.”
“We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen,” he said.
News of a potential acquisition emerged on Friday when Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike was circling Zscaler, which had a market value of about $32 billion as of Friday.
Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 shares of CrowdStrike common stock for each share of Zscaler common stock, or $260.41 per Zscaler share. Existing CrowdStrike shareholders are expected to own approximately 84.1% of Zscaler once the deal closes.
CrowdStrike said the acquisition would allow it to sell its platforms to Zscaler’s 8,000 customers, including 50 percent of the Fortune 500. The company explained that while CrowdStrike’s tools focus on securing endpoints and data, Zscaler’s products are adept at “securing the connections between them.”
“With Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter network security, cybersecurity’s largest single addressable market segment,” a company spokesperson explained.
Chaudhry warned that AI agents are “rapidly becoming the new weakest link” and said the deal with CrowdStrike will accelerate their ability to expand their zero trust tools to a larger customer base.
“We see a significant opportunity to offer customers far superior protection in a rapidly evolving threat landscape and enable enterprises to safely adopt AI,” he said.
Zscaler’s products will be sold through CrowdStrike’s system of resellers and distributors.
Both companies released their quarterly earnings reports on Monday, with Zscaler reporting $949.3 million in revenue for the first quarter — a 20% increase compared to last year’s first quarter.
The $43.9 billion figure tops last year’s largest deal, when Google purchased cloud security company Wiz for $32 billion.

articles.title: Norway says hackers exploited Microsoft security flaw to attack energy firms Equinor, Skagerak Energi
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Norwegian energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi were affected by a Microsoft cloud security vulnerability that hackers have exploited to target sensitive credentials, Norway's cybersecurity authorities said.
articles.full_text:
Norway says hackers exploited Microsoft security flaw to attack energy firms Equinor, Skagerak Energi
Editor's note: This article was updated with comment from Microsoft at 1:00 p.m. EST on Monday.
Norwegian energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi are among the organizations affected by a Microsoft cloud security vulnerability that hackers have exploited to target sensitive credentials, Norway's cybersecurity authorities said.
The vulnerability affected Azure API Management (APIM), a Microsoft service that allows organizations to manage and secure connections between applications and other systems. According to Norway's National Security Authority (NSM), an unidentified threat actor has been actively targeting access tokens and other sensitive information stored in the platform.
Equinor, one of Europe's largest natural gas suppliers, and electricity producer Skagerak Energi both reported cyberattacks last week.
The vulnerability was first discovered by Norway's energy sector, with Equinor playing a key role in identifying the issue and alerting authorities, the agency said on Friday.
Equinor said it detected the attack last Tuesday but did not fully contain it until Friday. The incident disrupted some internal services, although the company's oil and gas production continued normally.
"There is no indication that data has been stolen or altered," Equinor said in its latest statement, adding that the attack did not appear to have specifically targeted the company.
Skagerak Energi, which produces and distributes electricity and is majority-owned by Norway's state-owned renewable energy company Statkraft, disclosed a separate cyberattack on Wednesday.
The company said the incident had not affected its operations or electricity production and that it had found no indication that information had been compromised.
In a non-public security advisory reportedly sent to customers and shared by a purported recipient on Reddit, Microsoft said it discovered on November 18 a security issue affecting the older “Classic” tiers of Azure API Management and closed the access path the following day.
Microsoft warned that hackers may have accessed passwords and other sensitive information stored in vulnerable APIM systems before the company discovered the issue.
The problem mainly affected customers who had not followed Microsoft's security recommendations or had stored sensitive information directly in APIM instead of using Azure Key Vault, a separate service designed to keep such data secure. Newer versions of APIM were not affected, the company said.
Microsoft did not disclose how many customers may have been exposed or whether the same threat actor was responsible for the incidents involving the Norwegian energy companies.
On Saturday, Microsoft published guidance explaining how affected customers could identify and replace potentially exposed credentials. The guidance did not explicitly acknowledge the vulnerability or link it to the Norwegian attacks.
Microsoft told Recorded Future News it had identified and fixed a security flaw affecting several tiers of its Azure API Management service, including Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium. The company said it had notified potentially affected customers and provided guidance on how to protect their systems. A company spokesperson said they could not provide further details.
Norwegian authorities said the vulnerability affected organizations across multiple sectors in Norway and abroad.
"It remains unclear how extensively the vulnerability is being exploited or has been exploited in the past," said Martin Albert-Hoff, NSM's director of operational cybersecurity.
He added that authorities had found no evidence that successful or attempted compromises had disrupted services at Norwegian organizations.
NSM warned that more hackers could try to exploit the vulnerability now that it is publicly known and urged organizations using Azure API Management to take steps to protect their systems.
"The national cyber risk level is high," Albert-Hoff said. "Incidents in recent weeks confirm that the risk of cyber operations remains elevated."

articles.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
articles.snippet: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use "advanced cryptographic tools" to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
articles.full_text:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”
But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].
The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.
The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.
The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.
Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.
A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.
But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.
“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”
Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.
In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.
“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”
The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.
“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”
Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.
“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”
The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.
Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

articles.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
articles.snippet: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
articles.full_text:
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.
Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.
“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”
Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”
“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”
Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.
One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.
Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.
“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”
Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.
“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”
How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.
The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.
“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”
Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.
Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?
Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.
Using an A/B testing platform as the delivery mechanism is a genuinely uncomfortable escalation: the tool that decides which visitors see which experience was never modeled as a malware distribution channel, so none of the usual detections fire. The operational discipline angle is what stands out – attackers versioning and measuring payloads like product features means defenders need the same rigor about what their third-party tags are allowed to change. Supply-chain reviews for marketing stacks rarely get the scrutiny payments or auth integrations do; this will change that.

articles.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
articles.snippet: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
articles.full_text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).
Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.
The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.
The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.
Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].
Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.
The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.
IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.
Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.
The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.
Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.
Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.
A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.
That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.
More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.
Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.
Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.snippet: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.
This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.
According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.
Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.
Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.
“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”
Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.
Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.
Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).
“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”
Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates.
